title: Baking soda meets vinegar
interaction: A beaker of vinegar particles. One control: how many spoonfuls of baking soda to tip in. Each baking-soda particle that meets a vinegar particle turns into a bubble of gas that rises out of the beaker, and a counter tallies the bubbles. Tip in more soda than there is vinegar and the fizzing stops with white powder left on the bottom; pour in more vinegar instead and the powder all goes. A second run puts the gas to work: the same fizz inflates a balloon over the bottle neck, or lifts a muffin batter in a warm oven, where baking powder is baking soda sold with its own dry acid.
takeaway: The fizz is a new substance, a gas, made one particle from one particle, so it stops the moment either ingredient runs out, and the leftovers can never be turned back into vinegar and powder.
needsSource: none
pitfall: The bubbles are not air that was hiding in the powder, and the fizzing does not go on for ever: the amount of gas is fixed by whichever ingredient runs out first.
why: NGSS 5-PS1-4 (does mixing two substances make a new substance; baking soda and vinegar is the named example): https://www.nextgenscience.org/dci-arrangement/5-ps1-matter-and-its-interactions
overlapWith: acids-bases: that page titrates an acid with a base and tracks pH on a logarithmic scale; this page counts particles and bubbles with no pH at all, and the leftover powder is the point.

title: Bubbles and foam
interaction: A wand and a dish of liquid. Dip and blow: with plain water the film snaps back before it can close; with soapy water a film stretches, pinches off and pulls itself round. The film is a mesh of points pulled by surface tension that the reader can poke and watch spring back into a sphere; press two bubbles together and a flat wall forms between them; swap in a square wand and the bubble still comes out round. Last, whip the soapy water into a foam and scrub time to watch the walls drain thin and the bubbles pop from the top down.
takeaway: A bubble is a skin of water that soap lets stretch, and the skin pulls itself into the shape with the least surface for the air inside, a sphere, whatever the wand's shape.
needsSource: none; a surface-tension spring-mesh film model
pitfall: Soap does not make the film stronger; it makes it stretchier and slower to drain. And a bubble is not round because of the wand or because air 'pushes equally': the film shrinks to the smallest surface it can.
why: Children's Museum of Sonoma County, 'Bubble science facts for kids' (why bubbles are round, why plain water will not bubble): https://www.cmosc.org/the-science-of-bubbles-for-kids/
overlapWith: states-of-matter: it shares the particle look, but no existing page shows surface tension or a film; this page's whole model is a film pulling itself into the least surface.

title: Why a cake rises (and sinks)
interaction: Step through a cake from batter to cooling, with the bubbles of gas from the baking powder drawn inside the batter: the oven's heat makes each bubble swell; the batter around them stiffens as it reaches its setting heat; the cake cools. The only control is a scrub bar for oven time, with a door that can be opened at any point. Open it early and the bubbles shrink before their walls have set and the middle sinks; add too much baking powder and the bubbles grow faster than the walls can hold and the top collapses. The model tracks every bubble's size against temperature and the firmness of the batter around it.
takeaway: A cake rises because gas bubbles swell in the heat and the batter sets around them; let it cool before the walls have set and the bubbles shrink and the middle falls.
needsSource: none; gas expansion with temperature plus a setting temperature for egg and starch, stated as a simplification
pitfall: The rise does not come from the batter 'cooking up': it comes from gas already inside it expanding, and more leavening does not make a taller cake.
why: Demand: 'why did my cake sink in the middle' is a perennial search question, e.g. https://www.kitchenaid.com/pinch-of-help/stand-mixers/why-did-my-cake-sink-in-the-middle.html; curriculum: NGSS 2-PS1-4 / MS-PS1-4 (heating changes materials, some irreversibly).
overlapWith: states-of-matter: that page shows gas particles spreading out when heated; here the expanding gas is trapped in bubbles racing against a batter that is setting around them.

title: How a candle burns
interaction: Step through Faraday's candle: light the wick and watch the heat melt a cup of wax, the liquid climb the wick, the wax turn to vapour at the top and the vapour burn in a cone whose colour shows where it is hottest. Scrub a probe up and down the flame to read its temperature and see what is burning where. Blow it out and bring a match to the trail of smoke: the flame jumps back down the trail to the wick. One control per step: the lighter, the probe, the breath.
takeaway: It is the wax that burns, not the wick, and it burns only once the heat has turned it into a gas, which is why a flame can relight down a trail of smoke.
needs: Faraday, The Chemical History of a Candle, for the demonstrations (Project Gutenberg #14474, public domain); flame temperature zones from a textbook table.
needsSource: Project Gutenberg #14474, public domain; a few flame temperatures from standard references
pitfall: The wick is not the fuel; it is the pipe. And the wax does not burn as a liquid: the flame sits above the wick where the wax has become a gas.
why: Faraday's Royal Institution lectures for young audiences, still the canonical kitchen-chemistry demonstration: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/14474; England KS3 chemistry lists combustion among chemical reactions.
overlapWith: states-of-matter: that page melts and boils one substance in a box; here the three states of wax are stages in a flame that keeps itself going, and the burning gas is the point.

title: A candle under a jar
interaction: Step through what a candle does: the flame melts the wax, the wick draws it up, the wax turns to vapour and joins with oxygen from the air, and the atoms are counted before and after as they regroup into water vapour and carbon dioxide, giving off light and heat. Lower a jar over the flame and watch the oxygen particles in the jar run down until the flame dims and goes out. Pick a bigger jar and the flame lasts longer; put the sealed jar on a scale and the reading never changes.
takeaway: Burning joins the fuel with oxygen from the air into new gases, so a flame needs air and dies when the oxygen runs low, while every atom is still there afterwards.
pitfall: It is the wax that burns, not the wick, and the jar does not run out of 'air': carbon dioxide and water vapour take the oxygen's place. The wax has not vanished; its atoms left as gases, which is why the sealed jar weighs the same.

needsSource: none; oxygen in the jar consumed at a rate that follows the flame, extinction when the oxygen share drops too low, atom counting from the balanced reaction.

title: Sugar syrup and caramel
interaction: A pan of sugar and water on the stove with a thermometer. Step through the boil: at first the thermometer sticks at the boiling point of water; as water boils away the reading climbs and a gauge shows how much water is left in the pan; at each stage a drop of syrup is dropped into cold water and shown (thread, soft ball, hard crack); with the water gone the sugar itself starts to brown and finally smoke. A scrub bar is the only control, and the thermometer reading is computed from the real link between water left and boiling point.
takeaway: A candy thermometer is really measuring how much water is left in the syrup, and only when it is all gone does the sugar turn to caramel.

title: Cooking an egg
interaction: An egg in cross-section in a pan of water. One control: drag the thermometer. Inside the white and the yolk, proteins drawn as curled-up strings unfold as the heat rises and tangle with their neighbours; the white turns from clear to cloudy to firm at a lower heat than the yolk, so dragging slowly gives a runny yolk in a set white, and holding at a hard boil for long gives a rubbery white and a grey ring. Drag the thermometer back down and nothing uncurls.
takeaway: Heat makes an egg's proteins unfold and tangle together, the white a little before the yolk, and once tangled they never go back, which is why a cooked egg cannot be uncooked.
needs: Setting temperatures of the main egg-white proteins and of yolk (ovotransferrin about 61 to 63 °C, ovalbumin about 80 to 84 °C, yolk about 65 to 70 °C), from published food-chemistry tables (e.g. Hervé This); a handful of constants, no dataset.
needsSource: A handful of published denaturation temperatures (food-chemistry references); facts, no licence issue
pitfall: Cooking an egg is not drying it or burning it, and the white sets well below boiling, so boiling harder only makes it tougher.
why: Exploratorium 'Science of Cooking: Eggs': https://annex.exploratorium.edu/cooking/eggs; NGSS 2-PS1-4 (some changes caused by heating cannot be reversed).
overlapWith: protein-folding: that page folds a chain by hand against an energy score at level 2; here the proteins only unfold and tangle with heat, and the control is a thermometer.

title: Dissolving: where the sugar goes
interaction: Drop a sugar cube into a glass: water particles knock sugar particles loose from its surface one by one and they wander off into the water, while a counter shows that every one of them is still there and the scale under the glass does not change. Warm the water and the cube shrinks faster; stir it, or crush it first, and faster still. Keep adding sugar until no more will dissolve; then try sand, which never does.
takeaway: Dissolving spreads a solid out among the water's particles without destroying it; warmth, stirring and small pieces speed it up, and there is a limit to how much fits.
needs: How much sugar and salt dissolve in water at a few temperatures (handbook values).
pitfall: The sugar has not vanished and has not melted; it is all still there, spread out, and the glass weighs the same. Dissolving and melting are different things.

overlapWith: states-of-matter: that page melts and boils one substance; this one keeps the water liquid and spreads a second substance through it, counting the particles to show nothing is lost.
needsSource: Particles detaching from a lattice at a rate that rises with temperature and stirring, then random-walking through the water up to a solubility limit; solubility values from Wikipedia's solubility table (CC BY-SA 4.0) or a textbook.

title: Dissolving: where does the sugar go?
interaction: A glass of water drawn as particles. One control at a time: drag the spoon to stir, drag the thermometer to warm the water, or tip in another spoonful of sugar or salt. Each grain breaks up into particles that wander off between the water particles until no more will fit, and the rest sits on the bottom; a counter shows how many spoonfuls have gone in. At the end, let the water dry away and watch the same particles pile back into grains.
takeaway: Dissolved sugar has not gone anywhere: its particles are spread out between the water particles, warm water takes more of them, and drying the water out brings every grain back.

title: Why wet things dry
interaction: Watch a wet T-shirt on a line lose water one particle at a time: only the fastest particles at the surface escape, long before the water is anywhere near boiling, and a thermometer in the cloth dips a little as they leave. Turn up the sun, or the wind, or spread the shirt out instead of leaving it bunched, and the drying time falls. Hang it in a steamy bathroom and the drying almost stops; finally let a runner sweat and feel the same cooling.
takeaway: Water dries by its fastest particles escaping from the surface one at a time, so warmth, wind and a bigger surface speed it up and what is left is a little cooler.
pitfall: A puddle does not need to boil to disappear, and the water is not gone: it has joined the air and will come back as dew or rain. Drying in a draught is not the wind 'blowing the water away' but carrying the escaped particles off so more can leave.
why: KS2 Year 4 'States of matter' (the part played by evaporation and condensation in the water cycle; associate the rate of evaporation with temperature) https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study
overlapWith: states-of-matter: that page boils a box of molecules by raising the temperature past boiling; this one stays below boiling and shows escape from a surface, the effect of wind and humidity, and the cooling of what remains.
needsSource: none; a molecular box with the hottest surface particles escaping (Boltzmann-weighted), the escaped ones blown away or allowed to build up as humidity, and the heat they carry off cooling the rest.

title: What a fire needs
interaction: A candle under a glass jar, with the air drawn as particles: the flame eats oxygen particles, the oxygen counter falls, the flame shrinks, and it goes out with most of the air still in the jar. One control at a time: the size of the jar, a gap under its rim, a lid, a splash of water that cools the wick, a wet cloth, or cutting the wick short. Each run shows which of the three things (fuel, heat, air) the move took away and how many seconds the flame lasted.
takeaway: A fire needs fuel, heat and air all at once, and taking away any one of them puts it out, which is why a jar snuffs a candle long before the air inside is gone.
needsSource: none; the oxygen fraction below which a candle flame fails (roughly 16 per cent) is a single published fire-science figure
pitfall: A candle under a jar does not use up all the oxygen: it goes out when the oxygen drops below what the flame needs, with most of the air still there, and the water that climbs into an upturned jar afterwards is mostly the cooling air shrinking.

overlapWith: reaction-rates-equilibrium: that page collides particles over an energy barrier at level 2; here the only question is which of three ingredients is missing, counted in oxygen particles and seconds.

title: Fizz, balloons & where the gas comes from

Watch a scale under the bottle: sealed with the balloon it does not move, with the balloon off it falls as gas escapes. Change the amount of vinegar or of soda and see the fizz stop as soon as one of them runs out; warm the vinegar to make it go faster.

title: Why fizzy drinks go flat
interaction: A sealed bottle holds carbon dioxide particles dissolved through the drink and crowded into the gap under the cap; a fizz meter counts the dissolved ones. Open the cap and the gap's push drops, dissolved gas climbs out as bubbles and the meter falls. Chill the bottle to keep more gas in, warm it to lose more, shake a sealed bottle and see that nothing is lost until it is opened; drop in a rough sweet and watch bubbles start all over its surface.
takeaway: Fizz is gas squeezed into a drink under pressure; opening the bottle lets it out, warm drinks lose it faster, and rough surfaces give bubbles places to start.

title: Growing crystals
interaction: A jar of hot sugar water with a string hanging in it. One control: how fast the jar cools. As the water cools it holds fewer sugar particles, and they settle onto the string one by one, each finding a spot that lines up with its neighbours, while a readout follows the size of the biggest crystal. Cool it fast and hundreds of tiny crystals appear everywhere at once; cool it slowly and a few big ones grow over days. Switch to salt water left to dry on a plate and watch cubes form.
takeaway: Crystals grow one particle at a time onto a neat stack, and the slower the solution cools, the fewer and bigger the crystals.

needsSource: A dozen tabulated solubility values (CRC Handbook / IUPAC-NIST Solubility Data Series); facts, no dataset licence
pitfall: Crystals are not alive and do not grow from the inside: they grow by particles landing on the outside, which is why they stop when the solution is used up.

title: A kitchen thermometer, from freezer to oven
interaction: One tall thermometer from the freezer to a hot oven, with shelves of everyday things beside it: ice, butter, chocolate, an egg, a pan of water, a pan of sugar, oil, bread. title: The lemon battery
interaction: A workbench with lemons, copper coins, zinc nails, wires, a small light and a meter. Push one coin and one nail into a lemon and the meter shows a small push, under one volt; swap the nail for a second copper coin and it drops to nothing; try other pairs of metals. Wire lemons in a chain and the pushes add up until the light glows; wire two such chains side by side and the light lasts longer instead. Inside each lemon, a cutaway shows the zinc slowly dissolving as the current flows.
takeaway: Two different metals in a lemon make a small push of electricity, more lemons in a row push harder, and the lemon is not the fuel: the zinc is, which is why it slowly disappears.

title: Why popcorn pops
interaction: A pan with one kernel in cross-section and a hundred more around it. Heat is the only control. Inside the kernel the water turns to steam and a pressure gauge climbs as the kernel warms, until the hull can hold no more and bursts, the starch puffing into a white flake; a counter tallies popped kernels against time. Swap the kernel for a cracked one and it only hisses; dry a kernel out and it never pops; turn the heat to full and the outside burns before the inside has warmed.

R. Soc. Interface 2015, DOI 10.1098/rsif.2014.1247 (full text on HAL; the journal's open-access status not confirmed).

title: Rust

title: Salt on ice: roads and ice cream
interaction: A block of ice drawn as a neat stack of water particles, with a thermometer. One control at a time: sprinkle salt, and salt particles get between the water particles at the surface so the stack cannot re-form, and the ice melts although the thermometer reads below freezing; turn the cold down further and the salt stops working; pour on more salt and watch where it stops helping. title: Sink or float
interaction: A tank of water and a shelf of same-size blocks: cork, wood, ice, candle wax, plastic, brick, aluminium, steel.
